James Stephen
jāmz stē'vən
n. (James Stephen, 1758–1832, barrister and Master in Chancery, legal strategist of the abolition of the slave trade)
Greek Stephanos, a crown; the surname is patronymic.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

James Stephen practised law in St Kitts as a young man, saw a trial of four slaves there which he never forgot, and came home a convinced abolitionist. He became a Master in Chancery and an MP, married Wilberforce's sister, and settled at Clapham. His contribution was strategic rather than rhetorical. War in Disguise; or, the Frauds of the Neutral Flags (1805) argued that neutral shipping was carrying enemy colonial trade in breach of maritime law; the argument persuaded the government to act against neutral carriers, and Stephen then drafted the Foreign Slave Trade Act of 1806, which prohibited British subjects and ships from supplying slaves to foreign and conquered colonies. It passed as a war measure with little opposition, and it destroyed perhaps two-thirds of the British trade before the abolition of 1807 was ever voted. Amo 5:24 is the demand his method served, that judgment “run down as waters” (Amo 5:24).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines chancery as a court of equity, and a neutral as a nation or state which takes no part in a contest between others.

expand to see more

CHAN'CERY, n. In Great Britain, the highest court of justice next to the parliament; a court of equity.

NEU'TRAL, n. A person or nation that takes no part in a contest between others; the state of being unengaged.

STAT'UTE, n. An act of the legislature of a state that extends its binding force to all the citizens or subjects of that state.

Key Scripture

Amo 5:24 — "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream."

Mic 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

Pro 31:9 — "Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy."

Exo 21:16 — "And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death."

Modern Corruption

He killed most of the slave trade with a wartime shipping statute before anyone voted to abolish it.

expand to see more

Stephen's 1806 Act is the least celebrated and perhaps the most effective single step in the whole abolition campaign, and it is a lesson in how righteousness is actually enacted. Twenty years of moral argument had failed to carry a general abolition; a narrowly drawn statute, framed as a measure of economic warfare against France, passed almost unnoticed and removed the larger part of the traffic. Mic 6:8 requires doing justly as well as loving mercy, and doing is a matter of drafting.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the man who finds the lawful instrument serves the cause as truly as the man who makes the speech, and usually gets none of the credit. Pro 31:9 commands judging righteously and pleading the cause of the poor and needy, and Stephen did it in the form of a bill. Exo 21:16 was the standing law behind it; his work was to make English statute reach the ships that were breaking it.

Usage

"“let judgment run down as waters” (Amo 5:24) — by statute, as it happens."

"“to do justly, and to love mercy” (Mic 6:8) — the doing is a drafting problem."

"“plead the cause of the poor and needy” (Pro 31:9) — he pleaded it in a bill."
